analysis.one_liner: Slashes sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, and mercury pollution from the nation's coal- and oil-fired power plants.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to cut power plant pollution by roughly two-thirds, with a 90% mercury reduction mandate, never left the Senate committee: it got one subcommittee hearing and died without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a national cap-and-trade program cutting sulfur dioxide emissions from power plants from about 8.5 million tons to 1.5 million tons a year, and cut nitrogen oxides through two regional trading programs. It also would have required coal-fired plants to cut mercury emissions by at least 90% and install continuous mercury monitors, with results published for the public. These pollutants cause premature deaths, asthma attacks, acid rain, and mercury contamination of fish.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who breathes air downwind of coal- and oil-fired power plants, which is nearly everyone east of the Rockies. The bill's own findings describe reduced premature mortality, fewer respiratory hospital and emergency-room visits, less childhood asthma aggravation, less acid rain damage to forests and lakes, and reduced mercury, which is a neurotoxin that builds up in fish eaten by pregnant women and children [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps total sulfur dioxide emissions from power plants at 3.5 million tons a year for 2012-2014, falling to 2 million tons in 2015-2017 and 1.5 million tons from 2018 onward, with the EPA allowed to tighten the cap further to protect public health [S3].

Establishes two nitrogen oxide trading programs with caps falling from 1.39 million tons to 1.3 million tons in eastern states and from 510,000 to 320,000 tons in western states by 2020, again with authority to tighten [S3].

Requires that emission standards for coal-fired power plants achieve at least a 90% reduction in mercury emissions as a category, and forces plants to meet maximum achievable control technology limits by January 1, 2015 if EPA misses its own deadline [S3].
Requires continuous monitoring of mercury emissions at every coal-fired unit and quarterly certified reports, with the data made available to the public [S3].

Keeps each excess ton a separately enforceable violation for every day it continues, with penalties set at twice the market price of an allowance, so violating plants cannot simply absorb the cost [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of coal- and oil-fired electric power plants, who would have had to install scrubbers and mercury controls, buy allowances, or switch fuels. Some of those compliance costs would eventually show up in electricity bills, most heavily in coal-dependent states.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal- and oil-fired power plant owners

drawbacks.text: Cap-and-trade lets a plant keep polluting locally by buying allowances earned by plants elsewhere, so some communities near large plants may see less direct relief than an outright per-plant limit would deliver [S3].
Most allowances would be handed out free to existing plants rather than auctioned, giving established generators valuable permits at no cost [S3].

The bill keeps the existing Clean Air Interstate Rule locked in place through 2011, which the bill's supporters framed as stability for utilities but which also deferred any tougher interim reductions until the new program started in 2012 [S3].

Compliance costs for coal-heavy utilities would be passed through to ratepayers over time, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge; the bill's findings argue control technologies were 'economically feasible,' but feasibility for the sector is not the same as no impact on bills in coal states [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and environmental gains are large and national in scope: the bill's own findings tie these pollutants to premature mortality, respiratory hospital admissions, asthma, acid rain, and mercury contamination [S3]. The costs fall on a specific industry and diffuse into electricity rates, concentrated in coal-dependent regions. The main design weakness is the cap-and-trade structure itself, which guarantees the aggregate tonnage cuts but not cleanup at every plant. On balance this was a serious, bipartisan attempt to fix the biggest remaining air pollution problem in the power sector.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in March 2010, and the committee never wrote it up or voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Carper introduced the bill on February 4, 2010, joined at introduction by 11 senators from both parties, including Republicans Lamar Alexander, Susan Collins, Judd Gregg, Lindsey Graham, and Olympia Snowe [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which was the last substantive action at the full-committee level [S1][S5].
On March 4, 2010, the committee's Subcommittee on Clean Air and Nuclear Safety held a hearing on the bill, printing S.Hrg. 111-1228, but no markup or vote followed [S5].

Fifteen senators had cosponsored by the end, split 8 Democrats, 6 Republicans, and 1 Independent, yet the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal- and oil-fired power plant owners came out ahead: they kept operating under the older, looser Clean Air Act programs and avoided the new sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide caps and the 90% mercury reduction requirement. Everyone downwind kept breathing the emissions the bill would have cut.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal- and oil-fired power plant owners

sides.party_line_note: Twelve senators from both parties introduced the bill together, and the final 15 cosponsors split 8 Democrats, 6 Republicans, and 1 Independent [S3][S4]; the bill died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed hard national caps on their sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions and required at least a 90% cut in mercury from coal-fired units, forcing spending on scrubbers, mercury controls, and monitoring. Those costs are the direct flip side of the public health gains.

Demand for scrubbers, mercury control technology, and continuous mercury emission monitoring systems would have grown under the bill's mandates. Their interest in cleaner air standards runs alongside the public's.

Deeper emission caps make coal-fired generation more expensive relative to alternatives, reducing coal demand at the margin. Cheaper electricity for consumers would have come partly from using less coal.
